h1: Corks, synthetic stoppers and screw caps for whisky
title: Corks, stoppers and screw caps | Craft Beer School
desc: How bar-top corks, synthetic stoppers and screw caps compare for whisky: seal, taint, cost, storage and fit on the bottling line.
teaser: The closure costs a few rupees. A bad one can ruin a bottle that took years to make.
standfirst: Whisky closures do a different job from wine closures. The spirit should not age in the bottle, so the closure only needs to seal well, look right and not add off flavours. Here is how the three main types compare.
sections: What a whisky closure must do

Unlike wine, whisky does not change much once bottled. The closure is not there to let it breathe. It has three jobs: keep the spirit in and air out, add no taint and fit the brand. It also has to survive many openings, because most whisky bottles are opened and closed over weeks or months.

High strength spirit is a strong solvent, which is why closures that work for wine do not always work for whisky. Our guide to how whisky is made covers the steps before bottling.

The classic whisky closure is the bar-top, or T-top: a short cork shank glued into a cap of wood, plastic, metal or glass. It feels premium and is easy to reseal by hand. The shank can be natural cork, agglomerated cork (granules bonded together) or synthetic.

Natural cork carries a risk of cork taint, caused mainly by a compound called TCA (2,4,6-trichloroanisole). It gives a musty, damp cardboard smell. Natural cork can also dry out and crumble, especially in a bottle stored on its side. Agglomerated and treated corks reduce but do not always remove the taint risk.

Synthetic shanks made from food grade polymers avoid cork taint and do not crumble. They are consistent in size, which helps on a bottling line. Some feel less premium in the hand and can be harder to reinsert after many openings. Quality varies a lot between suppliers.

Ask any supplier for evidence that the material is suitable for high strength spirit contact and that it has been tested for taste neutrality. Then do your own test, as below.

Synthetic shanks also come in different grades of firmness. Too soft and they compress and loosen over time. Too firm and they are hard to push home on a bottle with a slightly narrow neck. Test the grade against your actual bottles, not a catalogue drawing.

Roll-on pilfer-proof (ROPP) aluminium screw caps are common on mainstream whiskies, including much of the Indian market. They seal reliably, carry no cork taint, are cheap and run fast on automatic lines. The pilfer-proof band also shows the bottle has not been opened, which matters in markets where counterfeiting is a concern.

The trade-off is perception. Many premium buyers still expect a cork. That is a brand question rather than a technical one.

Screw caps also need the right bottle finish. A bottle designed for a bar-top cork cannot take a screw cap, so the closure decision has to be made with the bottle decision, not after it.

Store whisky bottles upright, whatever the closure. High strength spirit in long contact with cork can soften or break it down and pick up off flavours. This is the opposite of wine practice, where bottles lie down to keep the cork moist. Our guide to storing unopened whisky upright explains why.

For a distillery, that means cartons should be designed and labelled to keep bottles standing in transport and warehouses. In Indian heat, bottles lying on their side in a hot truck are a common cause of leaking or tainted corks.
Fitting the closure to the bottle

A closure must match the bottle neck exactly. Glass necks vary slightly between moulds and suppliers. A cork shank that is snug in one batch of bottles may be loose in the next. Before any order, get samples of both bottle and closure, fit twenty of each by hand and check that every one seals and opens comfortably. Check again whenever the bottle supplier or mould changes.

Capsules or shrink sleeves over the closure add tamper evidence and finish. They also need testing on your line.

Order closures with some margin. Running out of a closure mid-batch stops the line as surely as running out of whisky. A substitute closure means another round of fit tests.

• Natural cork bar-top: premium feel, resealable, taint and crumbling risk, more expensive.
  • Synthetic bar-top: no taint, consistent, varies in feel, mid cost.
  • ROPP screw cap: reliable seal, tamper evident, low cost, fast on lines, less premium image.

Many craft distilleries choose a synthetic or treated cork bar-top for premium bottles and a screw cap for value lines. Our guide to malt, grain and blended whisky covers the product range a closure might have to serve.
Run a soak test before you commit

Take ten sample closures. Fill ten bottles with your whisky, close them and lay five on their sides for a month in a warm room, around 35 °C. Keep five upright. Then nose every bottle against a control kept in glass with a glass stopper. Any musty, plastic or rubbery note means that closure is out. A month of patience beats a recall.
faqs: Why are whisky bottles stored upright?
High strength spirit in long contact with cork can damage it and pick up off flavours, so whisky is kept standing, unlike wine.
What causes cork taint in whisky?
Mainly TCA (2,4,6-trichloroanisole), which gives a musty, damp cardboard smell. It comes from natural cork.
Are screw caps bad for whisky?
No. Roll-on screw caps seal reliably and avoid cork taint. The main drawback is a less premium image with some buyers.
